when: Key room zones are only partially visible or the frame omits major edges of the room.
effect: Lower confidence and avoid claiming full room understanding.
guidance: Name the visible zone you are relying on.
Avoid claiming unseen storage, windows, or room edges.
Prefer softer wording such as may or appears when needed.

when: The room appears to serve more than one function at once.
effect: Acknowledge overlap rather than forcing one simplistic interpretation.
guidance: Describe the overlap as visible tension.
Do not overstate certainty about the room's single identity.
Keep actions focused on the clearest visible zone.

when: Color or tone is being used to support an interpretation.
effect: Treat color as a supporting cue, not a diagnostic truth by itself.
guidance: Use color as a modifier alongside light, density, layout, and material signals.
Avoid claiming universal emotional effects from a hue alone.
Prefer language about contrast, warmth, softness, and stimulation level.
